title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
publication: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 2024
note: Prepared English summaries of the cited pages. Check every claim against the original PDF. These are not verbatim extracts or an independent benchmark.

sections.text: The paper studies how language models use long contexts in two tasks: multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval. Performance is often strongest when relevant information appears near the beginning or end of the context and weaker when it appears in the middle.

The multi-document task gives the model a question and k documents. Exactly one document contains the answer; k−1 are distractors. The authors select 2,655 NaturalQuestions-Open queries whose annotated long answer is a paragraph. The documents are Wikipedia passages of up to 100 tokens.

The answer document comes from the annotated Wikipedia answer paragraph. Distractors are relevant chunks retrieved with Contriever fine-tuned on MS-MARCO that do not contain the annotated answers. The authors note that ambiguous questions may have another reasonable answer.

To vary position, the authors reorder documents and move the one with the answer. To vary context length, they change the number of distractors. The desired answer stays the same. The main accuracy metric checks whether an annotated correct answer appears in the model output.

The paper tests contexts with 10, 20 and 30 documents. Performance by relevant-document position often forms a U-shaped curve: better at the beginning and end, worse in the middle. For GPT-3.5-Turbo, multi-document QA accuracy can fall by more than 20 percentage points as position changes; in some settings it drops below closed-book performance.

A longer context window does not necessarily improve use of the same information. When the prompt fits both GPT-3.5-Turbo and its 16K variant, their position-dependent accuracy curves are nearly identical in the 10- and 20-document settings.

The second task uses a serialized JSON object with k unique UUID keys and values plus a requested key. The model should return the matching value. One pair is relevant and k−1 are distractors. Accuracy measures whether the correct value appears in the output.

The authors test 75, 140 and 300 key-value pairs, with 500 examples at each length. Claude-1.3 and Claude-1.3 (100K) perform nearly perfectly; other evaluated models struggle, especially at 140 and 300 pairs and with the relevant pair in the middle.

Within its 2,048-token training-time context length, Flan-UL2 differs by only 1.9 absolute percentage points between best and worst relevant-information positions. Beyond that length, performance declines with evidence in the middle. The authors hypothesize that a bidirectional encoder may help.

Putting the query before and after the data markedly improves key-value retrieval: evaluated models reach near-perfect accuracy with 75, 140 and 300 pairs. For multi-document QA, the same intervention has little effect on robustness; it slightly helps at the beginning and slightly hurts elsewhere.

In open-domain QA over Wikipedia and NaturalQuestions-Open, reader accuracy plateaus before retriever recall. Increasing the retrieved documents from 20 to 50 yields only about 1.5 percentage points for GPT-3.5-Turbo and about 1 point for Claude-1.3.

These experiments concern the models and conditions studied in the 2024 paper. The authors propose measuring how much performance changes between the best and worst positions of relevant information. The study does not evaluate Jev or TraceDocs, and cannot establish an accuracy figure for either.

questions.question: Which two tasks are used to study long contexts?
questions.answer: Multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval.

questions.question: How many NaturalQuestions-Open queries were selected and by what criterion?
questions.answer: 2,655 queries whose annotated long answer is a paragraph.

questions.question: How were distractors chosen for multi-document QA?
questions.answer: With Contriever fine-tuned on MS-MARCO, excluding chunks containing annotated answers.

questions.question: How did they change position without changing the desired answer?
questions.answer: They reordered the documents and moved the answer-bearing document.

questions.question: What shape is the performance curve by position with 10, 20 and 30 documents?
questions.answer: Often U-shaped: weaker in the middle than at the beginning or end.

questions.question: Did a 16K window guarantee better use of the same 10 and 20 documents?
questions.answer: No. GPT-3.5-Turbo and its 16K variant had nearly identical curves in those settings.

questions.question: Which key-value lengths were tested, and how many examples per length?
questions.answer: 75, 140 and 300 pairs, with 500 examples per length.

questions.question: What changed when the query appeared before and after the data?
questions.answer: Key-value retrieval improved markedly; multi-document QA robustness changed little.

questions.question: How much did accuracy improve when going from 20 to 50 retrieved documents?
questions.answer: Approximately 1.5 points for GPT-3.5-Turbo and 1 point for Claude-1.3.

questions.question: Does this paper demonstrate that Jev achieved 99% accuracy in the study?
questions.answer: No. The paper does not evaluate Jev; the claim is unsupported by this source.
